articles.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
articles.summary: Access to the burnt-out boat has been slowed by toxic fumes and lingering heat, the country's coast guard says.

blocks.text: The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.
More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.
Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.
The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.
In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.
"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.
"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."
Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.
A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.
The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.
The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.
Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.
"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

articles.title: Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia

image.caption: Zelenskyy's visit to Canada focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year. (Mark Bochsler/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday described the unfolding tension between Canada and the United States as a "strange" sight to behold, drawing a comparison to his own country's fight with neighbouring Russia.
Says Ottawa and Washington need to work out their differences
Zelenskyy calls U.S. threats to annex Canada 'dangerous'
In a wide-ranging interview with CBC News, Zelenskyy described American threats to annex Canada as "dangerous" and said both countries have a duty to resolve their differences.
"Strange," the president told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, speaking to the tension in North America.
"It's very dangerous [when] there are some problems between neighbours and we [Ukraine and Russia] are the example."

Russia and Ukraine are, like Canada and the U.S., neighbours with a lengthy border and history, though their current tensions are vastly different: Moscow's four-and-a-half year invasion of Ukraine is a deadly war, while the issues in Ottawa and Washington are largely economic.
"I think that the United States and Canada, will have to have … very constructive dialogue. They have to have it. It's dangerous. [There's] no choice," he said.
Zelenskyy's remarks come at the end of a visit to Canada, which was focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year.
He spoke about Ukraine's new strategic partnership with Canada, efforts to revive peace talks with Moscow and his view on any potential face-to-face meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelenskyy says war holds no 'win-win' scenario for Russia and Ukraine
100-year partnership with Canada

Canada and Ukraine signed a long-term strategic and political partnership on Thursday that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries. The declaration established a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.
On Friday, Zelenskyy said the length of the deal with Canada, one of Ukraine's most vocal supporters in the war, was chosen as a symbolic gesture.

"It's about roots," he said. "It says that we will be together for a long period of time. Our children and our grandchildren, we will work together. We will share the experience of security [and] a lot of different things."
Why Zelenskyy has no desire to sit down with Vladimir Putin
Zelenskyy's visit to Canada came not only as the relationship between Canada and the U.S. hit another low, but as the Trump administration renews its push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

After U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner discussed potential proposals to end the war during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, Trump said the Russian leader wanted to make a deal.

items: Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it

blocks.text: But on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed doubts the Kremlin is interested in ending the war. He said he believes Russia maintains its goal of occupying Ukraine, but said he would sit face-to-face with Putin if trilateral negotiations came to fruition — though he said he doesn't expect any movement until after Russian parliamentary elections on Sept. 20.

"It's not my wish … Better to sit with my family," he said of a possible meeting with the Russian president. He described Putin as an "enemy," but said sitting down with an enemy "can bring us closer" to peace.

Diplomatic efforts to end the war have been stalled for months, while both countries have escalated attacks on the other. Moscow has continued its bombardment of Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv has intensified its strikes inside Russia in an effort to reduce its economic ability to continue with the war.
"To be honest, there is no win-win in this war. It can't be so because [there's been] so many human losses. It stopped being win-win at the first day of this war between us," Zelenskyy said.
"The most important victory for everybody, it's not for Ukraine and Russia ... For the world, it's peace. To stop this war. And this is a victory for a human lives."
With files from Murray Brewster

articles.title: NSW police seize 36 illegal ebikes on northern beaches that are now destined for the crusher
articles.summary:
Officers found one 14-year-old’s ebike was capable of hitting 90km/h. Owners have two weeks to appeal the seizure before the bikes will be crushed

  • Get our

blocks.text: Dozens of high-powered and illegal ebikes have been seized by police on Sydney’s northern beaches just weeks after the force was granted new powers to destroy dangerous bikes.
The operation was part of a coordinated push with the New South Wales government to ensure people only ride legal ebikes that have not been modified to reach high speeds.
One of the ebikes seized on Friday belonged to a 14-year-old boy from Warriewood. Police said it was capable of reaching speeds of more than 90km/h.
NSW police said they seized 36 “illegal ebikes”. The operation was launched on the northern beaches “following following recent incidents of illegal, dangerous and reckless e-bike use”.
Assistant commissioner David Driver said police would be launching more operations across the state in coming weeks.
“Most ebike riders do the right thing and comply with the rules; however, police will enforce [the] new legislation if people ride non-compliant vehicles,” Driver said on Saturday.
In late August, NSW police were given new powers to destroy ebikes capable of exceeding the legal speed limit.
Owners of seized ebikes now have 14 days to let police know whether their bike was stolen and being used by someone else on Friday.
After that two-week window, the bikes will be “crushed”, the government says.
The legislation also allowed police to seize ebikes that do not cut power assistance at 25km/h, with non-compliant bikes to be removed from the streets.
The government invested in a number of “dyno units” – portable speed-testing devices – to measure an ebike’s power output.

blocks.caption: A seized ebike is taken away. Photograph: NSW police

blocks.text: The Transport for NSW secretary, Josh Murray, said one of the units was used on the northern beaches on Friday to inspect suspect ebikes.
“We can put an ebike on a machine and test its power and speed very quickly,” Driver said. “When they did that yesterday, the bike showed that just by clicking the throttle it could go over 40km/h.”

Ebikes have been hailed as a climate-friendly solution to city traffic congestion, transport emissions and even youth social media addiction, offering Australians a means to get more exercise and save money.
after newsletter promotion
But they have come with a cost. NSW recorded 226 injuries related to ebikes in 2024. In just the first seven months of 2025, that had already to surged to 233 injuries plus four deaths.
Murray said most people were legally using ebikes but a small group ignoring the rules endangered other road users.

“We are serious about ebike safety and operations like this will continue by NSW police with support from Transport for NSW to ensure all road users are safe and complying with the state’s upgraded laws,” Murray said.
“Ebikes must behave like bicycles, not motorcycles. If your bike can operate like a motorcycle under throttle or go more than 25km/h while being powered, it is not legal to ride in public.
“Before you or your child jumps on an ebike, please make sure it’s road-legal, otherwise you risk losing the bike.”
On Friday, police issued 16 penalty notices and 46 cautions for other road offences, including not wearing a helmet, using a mobile phone or having multiple people on a bike.

The new laws were announced days after about 40 ebikes and e-motorcycles swarmed the Sydney Harbour Bridge. Footage posted online also showed riders – including those on so-called fat bikes – travelling on the Western Distributor, and performing stunts.
That incident led the federal health minister, Mark Butler, to declare ebikes a “total menace”.
“We’ve got to make sure we stop these things coming into the country [and] police are given the powers to crack down, to take them away, to crush them, to destroy them,” Butler said in February.

articles.title: Martin Romualdez transferred to PGH for independent medical check
articles.summary: Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was brought to the Philippine General Hospital on Saturday morning, September 11, for an independent medical assessment that will determine whether he needs to…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 9:49am

An ambulance carrying former House Speaker Martin Romualdez leaves Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Sept. 12, 2026, as he is transferred to the Philippine General Hospital for an independent medical assessment.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was brought to the Philippine General Hospital on Saturday morning, September 11, for an independent medical assessment that will determine whether he needs to remain confined in a hospital or be transferred to a jail facility.
Romualdez arrived at PGH at 8:35 a.m. from Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, where he had been confined since his arrest on September 7.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division ordered the assessment as it considers Romualdez’s request to remain in a medical facility while in the custody of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP).

PGH doctors were tasked to determine whether Romualdez needs continued medical confinement. If they find that he does not require hospitalization, he could be transferred to the New Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory in Payatas.
The BJMP took custody of Romualdez on September 10 after the Sandiganbayan ordered the transfer of his custody from the PNP-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group.
His transfer to the Quezon City jail, however, had not been implemented as the court continued to hear his request to remain at Cardinal Santos.
The prosecution had opposed continued confinement at the private hospital and asked the court to have Romualdez assessed by independent government doctors.
Romualdez’s doctors earlier told the court that he needed to remain in a medical facility, citing fluctuating blood pressure and the risk of stroke.

Cardinal Santos team manager Dr. Rosalio Torres also previously told the court that Romualdez was at high risk of a possible heart attack. He said transferring him could compromise the “golden hour,” or the critical period when medical intervention is needed after symptoms appear.

During an earlier hearing, Cardinal Santos admitting physician Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan said Romualdez’s admission was unusual because he was brought directly to his hospital room instead of the emergency room despite complaining of chest pain.
Sibayan also said he was not allowed to enter Romualdez’s room to examine him, which he described as unusual hospital practice.
Romualdez was also reported to have exhibited signs of depression and anxiety. His doctors have told the court that he has been diagnosed with depressive disorder.
The PGH doctors were ordered to submit their assessment by September 13.
Romualdez faces a P7.44-billion plunder charge in connection with alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects.
State prosecutors accuse him of repeatedly receiving kickbacks and other pecuniary benefits from former lawmaker Zaldy Co on at least 15 occasions between 2022 and 2025.
Romualdez’s arraignment and pretrial are scheduled for September 14. — with a report from The Philippine STAR/Andrew Ronquillo

articles.title: Firefighters say this antioxidant helped them - their union warns it could be risky
articles.summary: Glutathione, an antioxidant, has been offered as a treatment at some of the largest US wildfires in recent years.

blocks.text: Days after he helped extinguish the Eaton Fire in Los Angeles, Pasadena Fire Captain David Marquez inhaled his first dose of glutathione on the side of the road outside the Rose Bowl stadium.
The wildfire became the second most destructive fire in California's history, killing 19 and destroying 9,000 buildings.
"We were having trouble sleeping," he said of his team. "Chronic cough, headache, fatigue - just a really rough set of symptoms following the fire."
"I felt much better immediately after the worst exposure of my career," said Marquez, a 25-year veteran of firefighting, who has battled with health issues for years.
"We were so desperate because of how messed up we were. We were willing to pretty much try anything," he said.

Scientists have long known that inhaling toxic smoke from a fire can cause a huge range of illnesses, including several types of cancers. First responders, like firefighters, are especially susceptible. Firefighters have a 14% increased risk of dying from cancer, external compared to the general American population, according to the US National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety.
And as awareness of the risks evolve, so too has interest in alternative - but often unproven and potentially dangerous - treatments.

Glutathione, an antioxidant that is naturally produced inside the human body, has been offered as a treatment at some of the largest US wildfires in recent years – including most recently in Spokane, Washington. Anecdotal evidence gathered by clinicians and fire departments has shown promising signs that it could be used to rid firefighters of some of the cancer-causing chemicals they absorb during fires. However, no large-scale research has yet been conducted on its safety and efficacy, and there are concerns over purity and contaminated supplies.

The International Association of Fire Fighters (IAFF) issued a rare warning about glutathione last month. It noted two recent recalls due to contaminants at compounding pharmacies that produce glutathione. It also noted scientific trials of other common, naturally-occurring vitamins that were found to increase – rather than decrease – the risk of cancer, although none of those vitamins are used in glutathione treatment.

"We don't know if glutathione is affective," said Sean DeCrane, the assistant to the general president for health and safety at the IAFF, which represents over 360,000 firefighters across the US and Canada.
"We don't know if it's a placebo effect. We don't know the long-term effect of this type of treatment."

DeCrane said his group opposes the way it has been "marketed" to firefighters, including in Spokane where morning briefings fire chiefs to their crews included suggestions that they visit a volunteer tent for treatment.

"The lack of research really raised concerns for us," he said. He adds that the IAFF has spoken to "multiple members who said that they did not feel well after the treatment, [and] that they felt worse."
"The clinician told them, 'Oh, that's just those metals leaving your body'," he said.
The recent rise of glutathione can be traced back to 2017, when a group of naturopaths formed together in Santa Rosa, California, to provide assistance to fire crews combating the Tubbs Fire.

The Integrated Health Action Network (IHAN), previously called the Integrative Healers Network, now sends volunteer clinicians to major wildfires across the country to provide glutathione, as well as other naturopathic treatments including acupuncture and massage therapy.
In response to the warning from IAFF, the group released a statement agreeing with the need for further testing, and offering to work with researchers to prove glutathione's effectiveness.

Co-founder Jen Riegle, who is not a medical doctor but is a licensed naturopath, external, said that glutathione treatment often leads to "clinically-meaningful improvements in headaches, fatigue and brain fog, which are some of the top symptoms we see in firefighters when they're on a fire". The treatments help to force out some of the harmful contaminants in firefighters' bodies, she claims, and can have short-term side effects immediately after treatment.

Riegle is hopeful the data the group has collected will spur on further research, and "to prove that this is a good long-term solution for firefighters". But she adds that all of the evidence IHAN has collected is anecdotal, and far from conclusive.
"I just want to be really clear that what we are collecting is data that we have because of a treatment programme," she said.

"It shouldn't ever be misconstrued as clinical trial data, or double-blind, placebo-controlled, peer-reviewed data. It is just meant as a starting point to be able to garner support for future studies." Medical trials of a new drug typically take years before receiving regulatory approval, and involve rigorous a research and standards.
Interest in glutathione rose last year when California's state Board of Pharmacy attempted to pass new rules that would have severely restricted its production.

The proposed rule change led to a groundswell of opposition from some firefighters, who travelled to the state capital to testify about how it has improved their health. The plan to further restrict it was later abandoned.

Marquez was among the firefighters who went to Sacramento to testify in uniform. He said he is grateful that glutathione is being offered more frequently – including by all fire stations in Pasadena, where he works.
He dismisses concerns about its effectiveness, including suggestions that alleviated symptoms could be due to a placebo effect.
Using an expletive, Marquez said: "I don't [care] it's a placebo - it was working. Guys were saying they felt better. I felt better. And it made me want to seek out more treatments."

Regulations and medicines for firefighters have at times lagged behind the need. Until last year, firefighters for the National Forest Service were banned from wearing face masks due to concerns about their ability to operate in rugged mountain terrains. There is now a growing understanding of the need for respiratory protections and decontamination to help prevent certain cancers that are more common for firefighters.

Dr Coralynn Sack, an occupational pulmonologist specialising in air pollution's effects on the body at the University of Washington, said the noxious fumes from wildfires are well known to pose "inhalational hazards" to firefighters.
"There's been a lot of interest in using antioxidant supplements for air pollution in general," she said. "Studies have shown mixed responses. Some have even shown worse responses."

Sack said there was "biological plausibility" to think such a treatment might work, but said she was "very underwhelmed by the data that exists". There have been no clinical trials on glutathione in firefighters, she added.
Sack said the debate over glutathione "shifts the emphasis away from things that we know work" like giving firefighters access to good personal protective equipment.

articles.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: In New York, the Pentagon and Pennsylvania, solemn ceremonies commemorate the landmark anniversary.
articles.byline: Grace Eliza Goodwin, Bernd Debusman Jr, Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu, Nadine Yousif

blocks.text: Watch: "We'll never ever forget" - Americans remember 9/11 at 25th anniversary
ByGrace Eliza GoodwinReporting from9/11 memorial in New YorkBernd Debusman JrKwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Nadine YousifCanada reporter
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.
Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.
Two beams of light illuminated the Manhattan sky for a Tribute in Light on Friday evening, as other landmarks in the state lit up in blue in commemoration.
Image source, Getty Images

blocks.caption: Fire Department of New York (FDNY) firefighters pay their respects at the memorial before a ceremony to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center

blocks.text: Image source, Pool/Getty Images

blocks.caption: Image caption, All living former US presidents attended a memorial in New York City

blocks.text: All living former US presidents attended a memorial in New York City

blocks.caption: Image caption, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick lost his brother Gary and several colleagues in the attack

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick lost his brother Gary and several colleagues in the attack

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Trump spoke at the Pentagon

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
President Trump spoke at the Pentagon
George W Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks, was joined by former Presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton at Friday's ceremony at the World Trade Center site.
At the Pentagon, President Trump attended a commemoration alongside cabinet secretaries and Condoleezza Rice, who was national security adviser on 9/11.
"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago," Trump said. "We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today."
He sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.
Trump told the crowd that the Islamic Republic "will never, ever have a nuclear weapon".
Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Wall of Names at Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The Wall of Names at Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania

Janice Brooks had only moved to New York a couple of weeks before 9/11 to begin what she calls "the biggest adventure", working for a company on the 84th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center.
She told the BBC she was in the office when the first plane hit the North Tower. While she was evacuating, the second plane hit with an "almighty thud".
Brooks said she heard "one of those horror film screams" as a woman was hit by debris. She looked up and saw a "big gaping hole" where her office should have been.
Every year on 11 September, bells ring to commemorate the exact time that each of the four planes crashed, and the exact time the Twin Towers fell.
Each of the six bells is followed by a moment of silence.
This year, a seventh bell was rung to commemorate the thousands who died from diseases including cancer after the attacks.
Illnesses related to dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have since claimed more than threefold the nearly 3,000 lives lost in the attacks, US health officials say.

blocks.caption: A ceremonial bell sits at the 9/11 Memorial during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks

blocks.text: As the names of the dead were read out for nearly four hours at the ceremony in Manhattan, a 9/11 widow criticised Saudi Arabia and what she characterised as failures by US officials to hold the kingdom accountable.
"You are missed more with each year that passes," Terry Strada said of her husband Tom Strada in remarks broadcast live worldwide.
"But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?"

items: You can listen to Terry Strada's story in the BBC radio documentary Intrigue: A 9/11 story

blocks.text: The comments by Strada, national chairperson of 9/11 Families United, drew applause from the audience.
The majority of those who carried out the 9/11 attacks were from Saudi Arabia and planning was led by al-Qaeda founder Osama Bin-Laden, scion of a prominent Saudi family.

But Saudi officials have repeatedly denied any involvement in the attacks, and in 2004 the 9/11 Commission Report "found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded" al-Qaeda.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Families attended ceremonies to honour the lives lost

blocks.text: Families attended ceremonies to honour the lives lost

blocks.caption: People gather at the National September 11 Memorial during the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks.

blocks.text: Events were also held elsewhere to honour the victims. In London, there was a ceremonial event at Buckingham Palace attended by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the US ambassador Warren Stephens.
The Toronto Stock Exchange also held an event to remember colleagues who died in the attacks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Buckingham Palace

blocks.text: Image source, WPA Pool/Getty Images
Buckingham Palace

blocks.caption: Image caption, Commemorations were held at Lloyd's of London

blocks.text: Commemorations were held at Lloyd's of London
In Gander, Newfoundland, the US ambassador to Canada praised the small town that took in thousands of passengers from 38 diverted planes in the hours after the attack.
"When people in America hear the word Gander, our hearts soften," Pete Hoekstra said.
"As a representative of the United States government, thank you for your friendship... to the nation of Canada, thank you for being a partner and for the shared sacrifices that you made with us."

His remarks come amid fraught relations between the US and Canada, with the two countries engaged in a trade war. Ahead of the 9/11 commemorations, some Gander residents had called for Hoekstra's invite to be rescinded.

Still, Hoekstra's speech was met with applause. But in separate remarks afterwards, former Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chrétien said: "I have message for American friends... never mistake our generosity for weakness." He received a standing ovation.
In Milan, a group of Italian and US firefighters participated in a ceremonial stair climb to honour the emergency responders who died in the line of duty.
Dressed in their uniforms and carrying equipment, they climbed 110 floors up and down the Galfa Tower, in remembrance of the number of storeys on each of the Twin Towers.

articles.title: Marcos arrives in India for BRICS Summit
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has arrived in New Delhi, India for the 18th BRICS Summit, according to the Presidential Communications Office on Saturday.

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 8:36am
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has arrived in New Delhi, India for the 18th BRICS Summit, according to the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) on Saturday.
The president departed from Villamor Air Base at around 7:50 p.m. on Friday, Philippine time.
“President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. has arrived in New Delhi, India to take part in the 18th BRICS Summit in his capacity as ASEAN Chair and invited outreach country,” the PCO said in a Facebook post.
The BRICS Summit is an annual meet between heads of state as a means of consultation and cooperation on different global issues.
Marcos vowed to carry the ASEAN’s voice to amplify the regional bloc’s perspectives. He said he would use his time to present the region's priorities to BRICS members.

“We will engage the BRICS community, whose ranks include four of our fellow ASEAN member-states, on advancing our quest for peace, inclusive growth, regional resilience, sustainable development, food and energy security, and a rules-based international order,” Marcos said in his departure speech in Pasay City.

“We will call for fairer global governance, stronger disaster preparedness, the responsible use of new technologies, climate action, and the peaceful settlement of disputes under international law. We will bring lessons from ASEAN’s track record and long-standing commitment to open and inclusive dialogue, while preserving strategic autonomy,” he added.
Marcos had been invited by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and is set to have a bilateral meeting with him. The President said that he will also meet with Indian companies and other key players.
This is Marcos’ second trip to India. In August 2025, he also went to India for a five-day state visit. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe
articles.summary: Art detectives and security experts say the number of museum thefts across Europe is increasing.

blocks.text: When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.
Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.

And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October.
The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.

"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".

Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna, Bronze Age artefacts in Spain, and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about.

The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.
Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.

Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.
Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats.
"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared to well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.
Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.
For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-century mansions in Langres.
"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains.
Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.
And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.
Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month, external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.
The increased aggression creates new security concerns.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.
What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so around 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says.
Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.

"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."
Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says.

After a theft, police generally have between four to six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators.
But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case.

On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them".

Christopher A. Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".
Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds.
After its theft in October, Maison des Lumières launched a security audit carried out by police officers appointed by France's cultural ministry, mayor Caviezel says.
Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed.

MAK in Vienna also increased its security to prevent "copycat offenders and to provide our audience with visible security", its director says. Entry is through a metal detector, and bags must be put in the cloakroom or in lockers, and there are more security guards.

Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.

"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."
Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine.
Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.
However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".
"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution."

Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.
Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months.

Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a UNESCO convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged.
The challenge for museums now is increasing security while also staying open to the public.
"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."
Additional reporting by Madeleine Lake.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak in Congo spreads to a 7th province
articles.summary: KINSHASA, Congo — The Ebola outbreak in Congo, the world’s fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record, has now spread to seven provinces in the African country, local authorities…

blocks.text: KINSHASA, Congo — The Ebola outbreak in Congo, the world’s fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record, has now spread to seven provinces in the African country, local authorities said. And it’s showing no signs of slowing down.

According to the governor of the northwestern province of Sud-Ubangi, Jean-Rene Galekwa Vundawe, Congo’s national research institute tested a sample and found traces of the Bundibugyo virus, the rare kind of Ebola that caused the current outbreak.

The statement, which was issued on Thursday and reported by local media outlets on Friday, said the sample was from the Bulu health district in Sud-Ubangi. It did not disclose other information about the source of the infection.

Local lawmaker and former health minister Jean-Jacques Mbungani said on X on Thursday a positive case was recorded in Gwaka, a town in Sud-Ubangi province. He said the patient was a 23-year-old man and has died.

Mbungani said in just three weeks the man had departed from South Kivu province — where confirmed Ebola cases have been reported — and then traveled to Rwanda and Uganda. He then traveled to Congo’s Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak.
He then traveled from the northeast of the country to the northwest through the provinces of Tshopo, Mongala and Sud-Ubangi, according to Mbungani.

Doctors and local authorities in Sud-Ubangi were alerted to a patient that had a fever and was vomiting blood, Mbungani told The Associated Press on Friday in a telephone interview, adding that the man had died on Tuesday. Samples were then taken after the patient had died and were sent to the national research institute.
“It worries me. … Our province borders Congo-Brazzaville and the Central African Republic. We fear it may spread regionally,” said Mbungani.

The development makes Sud-Ubangi the seventh province affected by the outbreak — and the first in western Congo — a worrisome spread outward from what was previously concentrated in the country’s east. A case was detected in Kinshasa in May in a person who had traveled from eastern Congo, but the Congolese capital, more than 1,600 kilometers (1,000 miles) away from the epicenter, was not classified as an affected province.
As of Thursday, 7,022 cases and 3,398 deaths have been reported, according to the latest government figures released Friday.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in Ituri province, the outbreak’s epicenter, but risen sharply in neighboring North Kivu and Haut-Uele.

The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions for aid efforts, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The situation is particularly concerning at displacement sites, where residents already live in extremely precarious conditions.

Sud-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic, does not border any of the six provinces in eastern Congo where confirmed Ebola cases had previously been reported. They include Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo and Bas-Uele.
WHO said last month there is a risk the outbreak could spread from Congo to the Central African Republic and South Sudan, which border the affected provinces.
Neighboring Uganda, which had reported 20 cases since May, declared itself free of Ebola in July.

Last month, Congo began vaccinating health and other front-line workers with the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type of the virus called Zaire.
Clinical trials are underway to find a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus.

The vaccination trials started in Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele provinces, Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC’s director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said Thursday. Vaccinations in Ituri are set to start next week, he added.

articles.title: As China rises, Australia is increasingly enmeshed in the US war machine. Is the alliance still worth the risk?
articles.summary:
Australia is being exploited by an ally that could draw it, however unwillingly, into war with China, experts warn

  • Get our

blocks.text: “Physical security matters,” said Kevin Rudd, at his axiomatic best before the National Press Club this week.
“Our first responsibility is to secure our people’s future in this most contested region of the world.”

Prime minister, to foreign minister, to ambassador, Rudd – on his self-declared, self-deprecatory “career trajectory towards infinitesimal demotion” – has an unparalleled perspective on Australia’s place in the world.
In a time of dramatic global upheaval, he argued, the nation’s security alliance with the United States was neither trivial nor sentimental.
“Our alliance with the United States remains a force multiplier for Australia’s defence needs.”

But, Rudd said, it did represent one of the seismic challenges Australia faced: countenancing “the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be in the future”.
Alliance with the US, he said, was necessary but not sufficient for the country’s long-term national security.
“We must also re-embrace national self-reliance to anticipate the full range of future uncertainties.” A Rudd sentence if ever one was said.
And the alliance, like any, carries risk.

Twice in a row, Rudd was asked whether Australia would even have a choice if the US were to become involved in a war with China over Taiwan, which Rudd judged a “one in three” chance in 2028 (the year of Taiwan’s next presidential election).
Or whether, in that scenario, Australian support would be automatically expected.

Both times Rudd declined to answer, even as he was asked directly whether – if US nuclear submarines were steaming from Australian ports, and US bombers taking off from Australian airfields, heading for Chinese sea and airspace – Australia could decline to be part of another American war.
“On Australian responses: I’ll engage in classic duck and weave,” Rudd said.
Growing enmeshment
This week, the Guardian published new data showing the US military and its defence industrial interests control, or have access to, more than 100 military bases across the Australian continent.
The enmeshment of the Australian military within the giant US war machine has hastened over recent years, and is set to grow even further.

US nuclear-capable bombers take off from Australian airfields on missions across the world – potentially carrying nuclear weapons (the US government won’t say, Australia won’t ask). From next year, nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines will port through HMAS Stirling off Perth.

The US remains Australia’s fundamental security ally, but it is also a country currently mired in what many international law experts say is an illegal, unprompted war, and one seen by many in Australia as a superpower in decline and increasingly unreliable.

The federal government maintains the US remains indispensable to Australian security. Marking 75 years of the Anzus Treaty this week, the deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the US “remains our closest ally and principal strategic partner”.
“For more than seven decades, the alliance has underpinned peace, stability and prosperity in our region and continues to contribute to the region’s strategic balance,” he said.

But a growing cohort of military strategists and geostrategic analysts argues Australia’s increasing enmeshment with the US military makes it less safe: that Australia is being exploited by an ally that could draw this country, however unwillingly, into war with China.
‘An automatic target’

David Vine, the author of Base Nation and The United States of War, told the Guardian the expansion of US military presence in Australia was of a scale unprecedented outside the conflicts in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq.

“What’s clear is that the US is preparing for war with China,” he said, “and for Australians, it’s worth thinking about whether they want to go to war with China, especially given Australia’s relative proximity.”

Australia did play – especially through Pine Gap – a significant role in the US global military system, Vine said, but the Australian military’s main role was as “a kind of auxiliary military force for the United States”.
Vine argued the current US-precipitated war in Iran had again demonstrated the “myth of the security umbrella” in hosting US bases.
“Hosting US bases turns a country into an automatic target; it makes host countries immediately complicit in anything and everything the US military might do, including waging war,” he said.
Instead of deterring potential adversaries, Vine said US military presence often escalated the risk of conflict.
“Building up US military power in China’s region and encircling China only encourages the Chinese military to respond in kind, to continue to build up its military power,” he said.

Vine argued that the breadth and scope of US military presence went far beyond any deterrent capability and instead demonstrated that the nation was preparing for a war that “frighteningly, too many people in the US military establishment assume is inevitable”.

“These are the same people who have been supporting a completely failed military strategy globally, who are making the world a far more dangerous place, and making it more likely that the United States and China and their respective allies will go to war.”
‘Every alliance is exploited’

During the presidency of Barack Obama, Dr Van Jackson served as a strategic adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, when Australia took on a new geostrategic significance, part of that administration’s “pivot” to Asia.

“That pivot was about many things in relation to China, but specifically the geographic encirclement of China … in service of war fighting contingencies against China,” Jackson, an associate professor in international relations at the Victoria University of Wellington, told the Guardian.
“At the grand strategy level, it was about ensuring American primacy: global primacy is the principal means and ends of US foreign policy.”
Australia, as an ally, represents to the US an immensely useful piece of geography.

“Australia is this almost-perfect location to be distant enough from the immediate battle space in a Taiwan or an East China Sea scenario, but at the same time, close enough for power projection, for flowing forces, and to function as a kind of rear area base for recovery,” Jackson said.

Jackson noted the US-Australia alliance was often phrased in euphemism, around “mateship”, of shared values and of a commitment to democracy. Australia’s unswerving support for the US was part of that rhetoric too, he said, citing Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of war at the Pentagon, praising Australia for being “with us, even in our less-advisable wars”.
While Jackson believed “that romance” was authentically felt, it was secondary to the US’ interest in using Australia for “very exploitative reasons”.
“Every alliance is exploited … and geography is the purpose Australia serves,” he said.

Given the size of the US military – America’s military budget surpassed that of the next six largest defence budgets on earth combined (including two countries that were actively at war) – the contribution of American allies “in terms of boots on the ground, or the share of aircraft or of frigates, is always a drop in the bucket”, Jackson said.
“When military strategists in the Pentagon think about alliances it’s always about needing access to bases, ports, and airspace,” he said.

“It helps on the margins to have these almost-symbolic military contributions from allies, but it’s not decisive in any way, it doesn’t really ever shift the balance of power, it’s not the difference between victory and defeat: it’s about access.”

articles.title: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
articles.summary: Mountaineer Mingma G tells the BBC about the climb to bring home the bodies of his closest friends.

blocks.text: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
Watch: Mingma G recalls the climb to bring home the bodies of his friends
ByCarrie Davies
Pakistan correspondentReporting fromIslamabad
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.

Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mingma G embarked on a difficult journey after learning his good friends had died

blocks.text: Image source, Mingma G
Mingma G embarked on a difficult journey after learning his good friends had died
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.

Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.

Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.

In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nirmal Purja was an accomplished mountaineer who put Nepalese climbers on the map

blocks.text: Image source, AFP
Nirmal Purja was an accomplished mountaineer who put Nepalese climbers on the map
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."

But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mingma G's old friend Kilu was among those who climbed Broad Peak with Nims

blocks.text: Mingma G's old friend Kilu was among those who climbed Broad Peak with Nims
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.

At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trekkers saw these climbers from Nims's group near the summit of Broad Peak

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
Trekkers saw these climbers from Nims's group near the summit of Broad Peak
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.

The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
Watch: Moment deadly avalanche crashes down Broad Peak
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.

One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.

Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Purja's coordinates according to Garmin's data. Mingma G says they did not find Nims's Garmin watch on his body

blocks.text: Purja's coordinates according to Garmin's data. Mingma G says they did not find Nims's Garmin watch on his body
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.

When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.

Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.

The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The recovery operation was carried out on foot because helicopters were not immediately available

blocks.text: Image source, Sirbaz Khan
The recovery operation was carried out on foot because helicopters were not immediately available

On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.

With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.

The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.

Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.

blocks.caption: Image caption, As news spread of the disaster, there were vigils in Nepal paying tribute to the climbers

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
As news spread of the disaster, there were vigils in Nepal paying tribute to the climbers
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.

Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The bodies of Nims, Kilu and Gyaljen Sherpa arrived in Kathmandu on 11 August

blocks.text: The bodies of Nims, Kilu and Gyaljen Sherpa arrived in Kathmandu on 11 August
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

articles.title: Palawan ferry fire death toll rises to 35; 53 still missing
articles.summary: The death toll from the ferry fire off Coron, Palawan has risen to 35, with 43 survivors and 53 people still missing, the Philippine Coast Guard said Saturday.

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 7:38am

This handout photo taken on September 11, 2026 and released by the Philippine coast Guard (PCG), shows an aerial shot of the ill-fated M/V June Aster with coast guard boats (L) at the stern off the shores of Coron town, Palawan province.
Philippine Coast Guard handout / AFP

MANILA, Philippines (Updated 8:52 a.m.) — The death toll from the ferry fire off Coron, Palawan has risen to 35, with 43 survivors and 53 people still missing, the Philippine Coast Guard said Saturday.
The latest figures were provided during the PCG's September 12 press briefing, a day after authorities recovered 30 cadavers from the burned vessel.
The PCG earlier said the fire aboard the MV June Aster was declared out at approximately 10:15 a.m. on Friday, September 11.
Authorities then conducted a safety assessment of the vessel, during which burnt remains were observed in the economy accommodation area.
PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the retrieval and transfer of the cadavers began at around 5:16 p.m. on Friday using the BRP Cape Engaño (MRRV-4411).
The recovered remains were scheduled to be transported to the Port of Borac in Coron, Palawan on Saturday morning, with an estimated arrival time of 11 a.m.
Cayabyab earlier said more bodies remained aboard the vessel after the initial 30 cadavers were transferred to the Coast Guard patrol boat.
The fire erupted on Wednesday after survivors reported hearing a loud explosion, followed by smoke and flames.

The fire erupted on Wednesday after survivors reported hearing a loud explosion, followed by smoke and flames. Cayabyab said that the fire spread very quickly, with "everything" happening within seconds.
The PCG earlier said burnt remains were observed in the economy accommodation area during the safety assessment.
The Coast Guard, Philippine National Police-Scene of the Crime Operations and other concerned agencies are conducting the recovery and identification of the remains.
The PCG also deployed oil spill booms as a precautionary measure after an assessment found no signs of oil sheen in the surrounding waters.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry's manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the Coast Guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country's more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.
The M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 sank along nearly the same route where 31 people died in 2023 after a fire broke out aboard the Lady Mary Joy 3 ferry.
Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., the company that owns the vessel, earlier said it was cooperating with the investigation. — with a report from Agence France-Presse
