articles.title: 'Canada is everyone, for everyone': Carney meets with Alberta remain campaigners
articles.summary: The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Friday Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a "calm" and "reassuring" presence for Albertans.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, centre left, and Forever Canadian founder Thomas Lukaszuk, centre right, bump fists after posing for a group photo with volunteers following a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Friday Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a "calm" and "reassuring" presence for Albertans.
Prime Minister shook hands with Forever Canadian volunteers on final day of federal cabinet retreat
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 11, 2026 7:20 PM EDT | Last Updated: 23 minutes ago
Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta, said Carney is showing "there is someone at the helm" by standing up for Canadians in trade negotiations with the White House.

Carney shook hands with volunteers from the Forever Canadian campaign on Friday in Banff, Alta. They were invited to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on the final day of the federal cabinet retreat.
The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.
The prime minister wrote "Canada is everyone and for everyone" with a black marker on the campaign's promotional bright pink recreational vehicle, which it's using to travel around the province.
The crowd then broke out in a rendition of O Canada.

items: Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward

blocks.text: Alberta is set to hold a referendum on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a second vote on leaving Canada.
Carney has called for national unity but has not gone out on the campaign trail to loudly make the case for Albertans to stay in Canada.

The prime minister did not take questions from reporters on Friday. On Thursday, Carney said he sees his role primarily as delivering on his economic agenda for Alberta and Canada to further the cause of co-operative federalism.
He also encouraged Albertans to get out to the polls next month.
"Canada is worth fighting for, and fighting for in this regard means showing up on the 19th or mailing in your ballot or participating in early voting," Carney told reporters on Thursday.
Lukaszuk said he expects there will be "a stage in the campaign" when the prime minister will become "much more personally engaged."
Lukaszuk also said he hopes to see the federal Conservatives get more involved in the campaign.

items: Federal Tories launch 'Conservatives for Canada' campaign ahead of Alberta referendum

blocks.text: "The leader of the Official Opposition, Mr. Pierre Poilievre, says that his MPs from Alberta are behind us. You know, I keep looking in the rear-view mirror of this RV. I don't see them," he said.
"But I certainly hope that they get engaged because this is not a partisan issue and this is the time where all hands are on deck."
Federal government acting as a 'strong partner': minister

While the federal cabinet chose to hold their meeting this week in Alberta and to meet with some of the province's mayors, ministers did not spell out any future plans to take part in the remain campaign.
At a closing news conference on Friday, Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, who represents an Edmonton riding, said it's not the job of the federal government to tell Alberta what to do.

"Our role with respect to this referendum certainly is not to tell Albertans how to do anything. It's not to tell Albertans how to vote. It is to make sure that we are a strong partner with Alberta, that we collaborate in terms of projects and other steps that we're taking to build a unified country together," she said.
Conflicting pictures of Alberta separation outlined by reports
Olszewski said the federal government's actions "speak a lot more loudly than if we just stand at a microphone and say some platitudes about Alberta."
But she also said her colleagues are "absolutely" calling for Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

"We are talking to Albertans about the importance of remaining in Canada," she said. "We're showing Albertans that Canada works, that we're doing our best to ensure that our country works for all regions across the country."

items: Calgary will be hit first and hardest by separatist debate, mayor says

blocks.text: On Thursday, Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas credited Carney and his cabinet for putting in "hard work" in his province and for not taking an off-putting approach to the debate over separation.

"If they had just diminished this to transactions, if they had asked Albertans, 'Well, what's it going to take to keep you?' then I think Albertans are smart. We would have been able to see through that," Farkas told reporters.

"They have been present not just in major events like Stampede but also ... visiting rural communities in Alberta. There's many areas of Alberta that haven't seen a member of Parliament from outside of the province — let alone a Liberal member of Parliament — in many, many decades.
"They're showing up to listen, to learn and to be able to support common cause."

articles.title: North Korea fires projectile toward sea — South Korea
articles.summary: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea fired an unidentified projectile toward the Sea of Japan on Saturday, South Korea’s defense ministry said. The South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it…

blocks.text: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea fired an unidentified projectile toward the Sea of Japan on Saturday, South Korea’s defense ministry said.
The South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launch toward the body of water that Koreans call the East Sea but it gave no details.
The report came a day after South Korea concluded five days of joint maritime drills with the United States and Japan that were focused on North Korea.
Late last month North Korea slammed plans for the so-called Freedom Edge exercises in international waters off South Korea as a “threat” to Pyongyang and other countries of the region.

In its last previous projectile test, the North fired a barrage of missiles into the sea on August 20, despite an overture from US President Donald Trump, who said he planned to meet this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

That launch from the nuclear-armed North came as South Korea and the United States held a shorter edition of their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises, following an order from Trump to scale them back.
Trump’s order alarmed US allies in the region, with the president calling the drills “inappropriate and hostile” towards North korea.
Pyongyang has long condemned US-South Korea joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion, often staging missile launches around the drills.
Trump, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with Kim in his first term, told reporters at the White House on August 19 he plans to meet the North Korean leader this year.
The US president also said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.
It was unusual for a US official to state a specific number on a classified issue. Seoul says the North has around 80-120 nuclear weapons.
Hours after Trump’s remarks, North Korea fired more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area towards the Sea of Japan, South Korea’s military said.
Hours after the launches, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, said Trump’s decision to scale back the drills with South Korea was Seoul’s punishment.

She called it in a statement “an evident disaster brought by the unrealistic and anachronistic security outlook” pursued by Seoul, arguing the South had a “master-and-servant” relationship with the United States.

articles.title: Xi heads to India for BRICS summit overshadowed by war
articles.summary: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in New Delhi on Saturday for a BRICS summit alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in New Delhi on Saturday for a BRICS summit alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided grouping.
The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.
But Xi’s visit will also be closely watched as his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
His arrival comes six years after a deadly 2020 military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said Friday it was “ready to work with India… by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences”.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.
‘Substantial harvest’
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi’s foreign ministry.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
“You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border… but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday — exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 — waving placards against Xi’s visit.
Modi on Friday embraced Russian President Vladimir Putin before talks. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, also in New Delhi on Friday, said that pressure on Iran “has reached a critical and dangerous stage” following the “military aggression by the United States and Israel”.
Modi and Pezeshkian also held talks.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
‘Big constraint’
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi are also to attend.
Brazil is representated by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva campaigning for a fourth term in October elections.
BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement — the expansion of BRICS — today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.

articles.title: Arrest made over the death of black woman found hanged from tree
articles.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Mississippi in August.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have made their first arrest in the case of a black woman found dead and hanged from a tree, and say they could soon take more people into custody.
Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Jackson in August, but police only announced they were treating her death as a possible homicide earlier this week.
"That arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion," Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said on Friday. "This case remains active."
Fortune's death has worried locals in Jackson, a majority-black city in a state with a history of racial violence and lynching.
During Friday's news conference, Brackney said the medical examiner had confirmed Fortune's cause of death was homicide, adding that a suspected killer would be charged with murder.
Police had arrested one man and "additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence", she said, adding that they had interviewed 15 people in the case.

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, told the BBC that she cried when the police called to update her about the arrest, saying: "I guess I do feel like a little sigh of relief...like a little bit of peace just come over me."
"I just hope that they've got the right person," she added.
The arrest of a suspect followed weeks of what Spivey and residents in Jackson described as relative silence and inaction from local officials.
Combined with the grim nature of Fortune's death and Mississippi's history of racial lynchings, the lack of information about the case had left the community in shock and fear.
Spivey earlier told the BBC she had tried contacting Jackson police several times over the last two weeks, leaving multiple voicemails, and had not heard back.
Brackney addressed the family's frustration on Friday, saying: "We have been in constant contact with the mother and the stepfather, as well as the biological father, throughout this case."

A letter Spivey wrote to officials about the limited communication and speed of the investigation was read during a public city meeting on Tuesday - the same day Jackson police made the announcement about a possible homicide.
"I'm kind of like in awe," Spivey said. "Like, I can't believe it. That was quick."
Fortune's death has been described by a member of the US Congress as part of a pattern of "possible modern-day lynchings".

This week, more than 50 members of Congress sent a letter, external to the FBI and justice department, saying they were "extremely alarmed by reports of black people found hanging from trees in numerous states" and calling for an independent investigation into suspicious deaths of black Americans.
So far this year there have been at least 10 reported hangings of black people in the US, they said, adding that there were more than 70 lynchings documented between 2000 and 2025.

articles.title: Conservative MP holds independent hearings into COVID-19 vaccine injuries
articles.summary: Over four days in Ottawa this week, the independent inquiry held by Conservative MP Dean Allison heard from witnesses who shared their personal stories of vaccine-related injuries.

image.caption: Conservative MP Dean Allison speaks during a press conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Thursday, June 4, 2026, to announce he'd be holding an independent inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Over four days in Ottawa this week, the independent inquiry held by Conservative MP Dean Allison heard from witnesses who shared their personal stories of vaccine-related injuries.
Government did not sanction MP Dean Allison's four-day probe in Ottawa
Over four days in Ottawa this week, Conservative MP Dean Allison held independent hearings into COVID-19 vaccine injuries.

The Allison Inquiry heard from 50 witnesses drawn from more than 1,400 applicants, according to a news release. Most were Canadians who came to Parliament Hill from across the country to share their personal stories of injury.
According to its terms of reference, the inquiry was intended to listen to Canadians and not "make findings of fact or to reach conclusions."
It did not hear from Health Canada and was unsanctioned by the federal government.
Allison, who represents Niagara West in the House of Commons, said the inquiry "was intended to begin a conversation that should've begun years ago."
"No matter what people think about [COVID-19] or the vaccines or public policy, compassion should never be controversial," Allison said on Friday as the inquiry drew to a close.

Over the four days, the inquiry heard from a range of witnesses including Drue Taylor, a 36-year-old massage therapist who called in virtually from Alberta because she said her doctor decided travelling to Ottawa could take too much of a physical toll.

"I actually haven't been able to fly or travel really at all since becoming injured," Taylor told the inquiry. "Any disruption to my very normal could absolutely put me back into a serious flare where I'm bed-bound for weeks to months."
'Really frustrating'

Taylor said she developed postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic nervous system condition that causes symptoms such as rapid heartbeat, dizziness, fatigue and nausea when standing up.

After a year and a half of back-and-forth with the government, Taylor said she received an initial payout of $45,000 from the Vaccine Injury Support Program (VISP) . She called her experience with the program "really frustrating," saying she's been in the program's appeal stage for years.

According to Health Canada, VISP received 3,557 claims and paid out over $21 million to claimants between June 2021 and November 2025. Of the 1,433 claims that were assessed by the Medical Review Board, 252 were approved.
To be eligible for the program, people must have experienced "serious or permanent injury" as a result of receiving a vaccine authorized by Health Canada.

items: Quebec man's COVID vaccine story spurs others to come forward

blocks.text: Following complaints about its administration, the federal government took it over in 2026. The government had previously contracted a third-party administrator, Oxaro, to administer the program, which was later transitioned to the current Vaccine Impact Assistance Program (VIAP).
"They were supposed to replace my income," Taylor said. "The original payout wouldn't have even replaced my income for that year as a professional massage therapist who owned her own business."
While most witnesses were Canadians sharing their personal injury stories, the inquiry also heard from others like U.S. Senator Ron Johnson.

Johnson used much of his time testifying as a witness on Tuesday to attack Dr. Anthony Fauci, who led the U.S. response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Johnson is part of a U.S. Senate committee that voted to hold Fauci in contempt — and to suggest the COVID-19 virus was manmade.

items: We may never know where COVID originated. Here's why

blocks.text: The origins of COVID-19 are a subject of ongoing debate in the scientific community.
Inquiry was 1st of its kind in Canada
Allison said his independent probe sought to fill a void in Canada where, up to this point, no such inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries has been sanctioned by the federal government.

According to the inquiry's website, "more than 30 democratic countries, including many G7 and Commonwealth nations, have launched major COVID-19 inquiries examining lockdowns, mandates, vaccines and government decision-making."
Some medical experts have called on the federal government to launch a full national inquiry into Canada's pandemic response. No such government-led inquiry has happened.
In 2023, some members of the public conducted their own hearings — known as the National Citizens Inquiry into Canada's Response to COVID-19 — which unfolded across multiple provinces.

items: Top medical experts call for national inquiry into Canada's COVID-19 'failures'
Citizen-led inquiry into Canada's pandemic response makes stop in Winnipeg
Feds should devise way to reflect on COVID-19 response, says Canada's chief science adviser

blocks.text: Last month, Canada's chief science advisor, Mona Nemer, said in an interview with CBC's The House that the federal government should come up with a way to reflect on its own response to the pandemic to better prepare for future public health challenges.
"I think we have to respect how people feel, and then we need to meet them and hear them and understand where things stand," Nemer said.
Between December 2020 and December 2023, a total of 105 million COVID-19 vaccine doses were given out across Canada.

Health Canada reported that 58,712 adverse event reports were made in that time — representing 0.056 per cent of all shots — and that 11,702 of those were considered serious, or 0.011 per cent of all vaccines given out.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: US marks 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Americans commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, remembering the shock, the dead and the sweeping consequences of the al-Qaida attacks on symbols of U.S. might and…

blocks.text: NEW YORK — Americans commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, remembering the shock, the dead and the sweeping consequences of the al-Qaida attacks on symbols of U.S. might and prosperity.

The milestone anniversary brought memorial rituals — wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names — and volunteer projects in tribute to a day that about half of U.S. adults remember as the most historic event of their lifetime, according to a new poll. On Sept. 11, 2001, al-Qaida extremists hijacked four commercial jets and crashed them into New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.

Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to the trade center to hear his name and all the others read aloud Friday morning. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago.
“Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” her son told her in a final phone call, she recalled. His remains, like those of many other victims, have never been recovered.
Trump attends Pentagon observance

The attacks brought down the World Trade Center’s twin towers — icons of U.S. economic power, and among the tallest buildings on Earth — and blew a hole in the Pentagon, the U.S. military’s fortresslike headquarters near Washington. The fourth plane was headed for Washington, officials concluded, but the aircraft went down in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew members stormed the cockpit and fought the hijackers.
“Sept. 11 reminded us of the terrible power of hate,” President Donald Trump said Friday at the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony.
“The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win,” added the Republican, who was in his native New York on 9/11.

Former President George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, attended the observance at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in New York, along with former Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden, and current Vice President JD Vance. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wiped away a tear as he revisited the place where the attacks killed 658 of his colleagues — including his brother, Gary Lutnick — at the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum laid a wreath at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania after hailing the courage of the plane’s passengers and crew: “The actions they took should inspire us all.”
At ground zero, a new tribute to those who fell ill
For Angilic Casalduc, attending the New York commemoration “helps to show you’re not alone.” She lost her mother, Vivian Casalduc.
“There’s no timeline for grief, and unfortunately, no one can say how you can grieve, but coming here once a year makes it feel just a little bit better,” she said.

Traditionally, there are no political speeches at the ground zero commemoration, where victims’ relatives read aloud the long list of names and added personal messages. They thanked first responders and the military, invoked religious faith, appealed for national unity and touched on the U.S. relationship with Saudi Arabia. The kingdom was the homeland of most of the hijackers but denied any involvement in the attacks.
Mostly, relatives spoke of, and to, loved ones — whom some were too young to remember.
“You dreamed my whole life for me, and you only got eight months of it,” said Trisha Pakkala, who lost her mother, Deepa Pakkala.
Kiersten Haub, who was 16 months old when the attacks killed her father, firefighter Michael Helmut Haub, said: “I carry you through every milestone.”

Besides moments of silence at key points in the attack timeline, this year’s ceremony added another moment to honor people who were exposed to the clouds of toxic dust released by the twin towers’ fiery collapse and have since died of cancer and other illnesses. Questions remain about how many people developed health problems linked to the dust.
The impact of 9/11 endures
It’s a reminder of how the attacks’ long shadow has reached into many corners of life in the U.S. and beyond.

The U.S.-led global war on terrorism included invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan — the latter Washington’s longest war — and detentions and harsh interrogation of terror suspects in an international network of secret CIA prisons. The U.S. found and killed al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011, but the accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed still awaits a trial 23 years after his capture.

The attacks changed U.S. air travel, led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, prompted new federal surveillance and intelligence-gathering powers and banking regulations and generated ongoing debate over the balance between security and freedom.

Sept. 11 engendered a culture of individual vigilance summed up by the slogan, “ If you see something, say something,” while a wave of patriotism propelled some Americans to join the military, fire departments and police forces.
Casey Kloepfer was 4 when his father, police Officer Ronald Kloepfer, was killed at the trade center. The son became an officer himself this June, wearing his dad’s badge number.
“It’s big footsteps to fill, but it’s definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honor him and be the best police officer I can,” he said by phone this week.
New York’s mayor comes under scrutiny
Amid the post-9/11 calls to service and appeals for national unity, the attacks also fanned mistrust, prejudice and hate crimes directed at Muslims.

In the quarter-century since, Muslim Americans have played a growing role in public life from statehouses to Congress to New York City Hall, where Zohran Mamdani is the city’s first Muslim mayor. Yet he faced some criticism for attending the anniversary ceremony at ground zero.

Republican ex-Gov. George Pataki and 9/11 victims’ relatives cited, among other things, past remarks that some of Mamdani’s political associates have made about the attacks. Former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, a Republican, also opposed Mamdani’s attendance, though the two shook hands there Friday.

Mamdani, a Democrat, said this week he loves the city and country and that he wanted the anniversary to focus on victims’ families, first responders and New Yorkers who helped one another after the attacks, which he called a “horrific act of terror.” The 34-year-old mayor was an elementary school student in New York on 9/11.
One victim’s son and namesake, Michael Massaroli, used his time at the podium Friday to deplore people “using this tragedy to spread hate” against Muslims and others.
“That’s wrong, and that does no honor to the victims here,” he said.
Times Square billboards pause advertisements

Remembrances extended far from the attack sites, including beams of light projected from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium and a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
Sept. 11 isn’t a federal holiday, but Congress has designated it both Patriot Day and a National Day of Service and Remembrance.

“One appropriate way to remember is by serving,” said Jay Winuk, who lost his brother Glenn Winuk and then co-founded the organization 9/11 Day with friend David Paine. The group coordinates volunteer opportunities and this year arranged for dozens of Times Square billboards to pause their advertising at 9:11 a.m. Friday.
Instead, they simply displayed the time.

articles.title: CIA releases dozens of presidential daily briefs on Bin Laden and al-Qaida from before 9/11
articles.summary:
The presidential briefing documents were declassified on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks

Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th…

blocks.text: Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detail intelligence that government officials had gathered about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended American national security.

The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of Bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were financed.

Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs – the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.

The documents range from a February 1998 file – prepared for then president Bill Clinton – titled “Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning Bin Laden and other Islamic extremists – to a 12 September 2001 report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over Bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” in Afghanistan, noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.

Briefers in July 1998 called it “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents”.
Two months later, a briefer wrote that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”, and that al-Qaida “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.

Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”.

Other documents detail Bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”.

About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials were aware that Bin Laden appeared to be misleading the Taliban about his reluctance to launch an unprovoked attack on the US. Briefs prepared for George W Bush in early 2001 focused in part on Bin Laden’s “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents”.

A report a month before the attacks indicated Bin Laden’s commitment “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US”, noting that the 1998 al-Qaida attacks on US embassies “demonstrate that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks”.

At that time – August 2001 – officials wrote of “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York”, adding that the FBI was “conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the US that it considers Bin Ladin-related”.

Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded.

In the years immediately after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted a lack of information-sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that yielded new positions, including a centralized director of national intelligence, as well as the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes domestic and foreign terrorism information across different government branches.

Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also on Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.

articles.title: Poll bet’s beer video bitter for some voters
articles.summary: PARIS, France —A prominent contender in the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron is facing accusations from anti-addiction groups of violating a law regulating the promotion of alcohol with a…

blocks.text: PARIS, France —A prominent contender in the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron is facing accusations from anti-addiction groups of violating a law regulating the promotion of alcohol with a video inviting French voters to join him over a beer.
Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal this week launched on social media what he called the “1,000 bistros” campaign, brandishing a half pint of beer in a traditional cafe.

“A presidential campaign is about big rallies, but I also want it to be about great moments like this—a table, a drink, and simple and unpretentious conversation,” he said in the clip against the background of traditional accordion music.

Attal, who served as France’s youngest prime minister in 2024 and is still only 37, hopes the campaign will give him the edge in a field of candidates that is crowded even just within his own centrist sphere.
‘Clear violation’ of law
But the Addictions France association said the video represented a “clear violation” of France’s 1991 law regulating the consumption and promotion of tobacco and alcohol.

Noting that Attal’s beer glass showed a prominent French beer brand, it warned that his video “may encourage alcohol consumption” and, thus, be in violation of the law which restricts promotion of alcoholic drinks on TV and now also on social media.

“We see Gabriel Attal walking with a beer, sitting down with it, clinking glasses … The problem lies in associating alcohol with conviviality,” said Mickael Naassila, president of the French Society of Alcohol Studies.
These are “not the right messages during an election period,” he added.
Bar-hopping campaign

The clip also raised hackles on the left, with hard-left France Unbowed lawmaker Antoine Leaument calling it a “disgrace” and noting that alcohol “is responsible for 49,000 deaths per year” in France.
But, as he pressed his campaign for him and his team to visit 1,000 bars, bistros and cafes in the eight months left until polling day, Attal insisted he had done nothing wrong.

“The French art of living also encompasses our brewing and winemaking sectors, cider, and so on. Does having a drink mean you are promoting alcoholism? Of course not,” he said in a bistro in the northern port of Saint-Malo.
An eager user of social media during his stint as premier, Attal will need all his tech savvy if he is to become France’s next president.
Most polls indicated that Attal, who has sought to distance himself from Macron and was bitter over being forced out of office, is not even the leading candidate among centrists. /das

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis take over strait vital to global shipping
articles.summary: SANAA, Yemen — The Iran-backed Houthis seized control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast and captured three strategic islands on Friday, in a lightning offensive that cemented their hold on a…

blocks.text: SANAA, Yemen — The Iran-backed Houthis seized control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast and captured three strategic islands on Friday, in a lightning offensive that cemented their hold on a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.

The developments are likely to deepen the Middle East war’s impact on international commerce, as Saudi Arabia shut down an oil pipeline following attacks, and after months of Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Following a week-long offensive that has left hundreds dead, government officials said the Houthis seized the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
A local official with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said on Friday that the Houthis had “completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island.”

A government military official later reported the group had also seized Greater and Lesser Hanish, the last two islands in the narrow waterway not under their control, as well as all of the neighboring Red Sea coastline.
“Everything that was under our control on the western coast has fallen,” the military official added.
A witness told AFP that gunmen were “deploying along the Bab al-Mandab shore and are driving around in military vehicles.”
The capture of the islands, particularly Mayyun in the middle of the strait, heightens the Houthis’ ability to attack Saudi tankers, which they have been targeting since July.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea ever since Iran’s Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their “resounding victory” on Friday.
Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at Chatham House, told AFP: “Now the Iranians don’t only control… the Strait of Hormuz, but they control the other most strategic chokepoint in the Middle East.”

Oil prices have soared past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday — a potential headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.
The Houthis’ military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait was “safe” for all but Saudi Arabia following the latest advances.
‘Great victories’
The Houthi offensive has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen’s civil war that began with the group’s takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.
Houthi supporter Abdulhamid Dhaifallah lauded the group’s “great victories” in and along the strait.
“They have been preparing for this front for four years,” the Sanaa resident said.

Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.
The Saudi energy ministry on Friday announced that attacks led to the closure of the pipeline — which it had been increasingly using to bypass Hormuz — adding that injuries were recorded.

“The East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions was subjected to several attacks on Thursday morning,” a ministry official told the SPA news agency, adding: “The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries.”
Before the Red Sea offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen’s north.
They have recently attacked government-held areas in Hodeida and Taiz provinces and swept down the coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and Zuqar Island, north of Bab al-Mandab, on Thursday.
Mohamed, 46, who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the historic city.
Dangerous conflict
On Friday, the spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili, said they had begun shelling areas along the Taiz-Mocha road, while residents told AFP they heard airstrikes.
While Saudi Arabia has also hit back with airstrikes and ordered troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognized government is based, it has failed to stop the Houthis’ advance.
Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha’s airport on Friday, while a local official said the city’s seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
“I think the Saudis have tried everything they can to avoid this war, but I don’t think they have any more choice,” said Al-Muslimi.
The ongoing exchanges risk reviving a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Yemenis and sparked one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Sanaa and forcing out the government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022. /das

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says drones launched from Iraq hit oil pipeline
articles.summary: RIYADH — Saudi Arabia on Friday said drones launched from Iraq hit the East-West pipeline and led to its closure. The foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh…

blocks.text: RIYADH — Saudi Arabia on Friday said drones launched from Iraq hit the East-West pipeline and led to its closure.
The foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused injuries and damage.”
“The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries,” an Energy Ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier.

“At the request of the Iraqi prime minister … [Riyadh] has chosen not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government … to prevent attacks launched from Iraq against the Kingdom and neighboring countries,” the Foreign Ministry said.
But it stressed that Saudi Arabia “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities and its inhabitants.”
Saudi Arabia said the attacks, which occurred on Thursday morning, had left several people wounded.

Since the start of the war in the Middle East, Riyadh has increased its use of this pipeline, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, to bypass the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran. /das

articles.title: Passenger train derails in France leaving at least 44 injured
articles.summary: France's transport minister says 180 passengers were on board the train operating the Rouen-Caen route in Normandy.

blocks.text: At least 44 people have been injured, including one seriously, after a passenger train derailed in northern France, local officials have said.
An 18-year-old woman was airlifted in critical condition by helicopter to hospital.
Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said 180 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.
He added that 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were being deployed to the scene of the crash on Friday evening near the commune of Cléon, just south of Rouen.
The cause of the derailment was not immediately known.
The local authorities activated a mass-casualty response plan after the crash shortly before 20:00 local time (18:00 GMT).
Photographs later emerged showing passengers leaving the crashed train, with French media reporting that three carriages overturned.
France's state-owned railway operator SNCF reported "significant disruptions" on its routes in the area. It said replacement buses would be provided.
The authorities advised the public to avoid the area.

articles.title: Weapons, spyware and AI scams: Anthropic exposes Claude misuse
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — Anthropic has released a 154-page report describing how bad actors used its Claude AI system for state-sponsored surveillance, propaganda operations and other activities.…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — Anthropic has released a 154-page report describing how bad actors used its Claude AI system for state-sponsored surveillance, propaganda operations and other activities.
Here’s a look at some of the cases, which have added to mounting worries over the risks posed by rapidly advancing artificial intelligence.
Spyware in Mali

A tech consultant in Bamako, working with Mali’s junta-led state intelligence service (ANSE), used Claude Code to build “Lakana 360” — a surveillance system capable of monitoring roughly 25 million SIM cards across the country’s mobile network.
The app, which Anthropic could not disable, can capture calls, texts and voice traffic, and even identify people by their voice if they switch SIM cards.
It can also detect who is using encryption or a VPN.
Kamikaze drones in Russia
A small team of likely freelance developers in Russia used Claude to build software intended to power autonomous “kamikaze” drones.
The drone swarm was programmed to pick its own targets and crash into them to detonate, without a human making the final decision.
In their programming, the team repeatedly picked a location in Ukraine’s Donetsk region as their target and used VPNs to circumvent Anthropic’s geographic blocks.

The developers claimed to have received funding from Russian government and military research programs, though Anthropic assessed the group as a small freelance team rather than an official operation.
Missile-making in Yemen
A group in northern Yemen used Claude Code to help build weapons.
The popular coding tool helped design software for a guided rocket, drew up plans for a long-range missile, and helped develop an even faster type of missile called a hypersonic glide vehicle.
To avoid getting caught, they split the work across separate conversations with the AI.

Anthropic says there’s no proof they ever finished a working weapon, but the group did test-fire one rocket. It apparently failed, because they went back to the AI afterward and asked it to help determine what went wrong.
Propaganda in France
Anthropic traced a fake news operation to LKM Company, a French advertising agency.
Using Claude, it mass-produced political articles across about 70 fake news websites in roughly 20 languages — publishing at least 8,913 stories.
Each site was given a made-up journalist’s byline and a fake Twitter/X account, boosted by hundreds of fake accounts posting comments meant to look like those of real people.
The operation flipped its message depending on who was paying, selling what Anthropic called “propaganda as a service.”
It targeted the U.S., Brazil and France, and did a lot of work on the Democratic Republic of Congo, generally favoring the DRC’s side in its conflict with Rwanda.
Influencing in the UAE
A UAE-linked influence operation targeted the Muslim Brotherhood and United Nations experts critical of Abu Dhabi’s alleged role in war-ravaged Sudan.
The operation used Claude to generate reports, advocacy materials, social media content and testimony on Sudan.

Anthropic said the operation centered on an AI persona known as “Deadshot,” guided by a command calling for “a coordinated transatlantic and regional operation to dismantle the Muslim Brotherhood globally.”

The operation also ghost-wrote official testimonies intended for delivery at the 62nd session of the UN Human Rights Council, drafting them under “specific restrictions” that the speeches should not mention the UAE.
AI dates in China
A China-based app studio built a network of more than 20 dating apps that claimed to be staffed by real people but were secretly run by Claude.
Over just two weeks in April 2026, Anthropic found more than 4,700 different Claude-powered AI characters chatting with at least 25,000 real users, sending about 2.36 million messages in total.
To seem more believable, real human workers were mixed in with the bots — roughly one human for every three AI personas — handling things the AI couldn’t, like video calls. /das

articles.title: France: Sabotage suspected in train derailment
articles.summary: Dozens were injured when a train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, on Friday evening. Police believe the accident may have been deliberately caused, local media say.

image.caption: The network operator said traffic on the line has been halted [FILE: June 2026]Image: Syspeo/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said, with local media citing police as saying sabotage may have been at play in the incident.

At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement.
One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added.
The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.
What else do we know about the train derailment?
French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.
Local authorities have urged the public to avoid the area.
The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.
"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.
​A police spokesperson said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.
A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports.

articles.title: Tiananmen activists sentenced to between 5 and 7 years in prison
articles.summary: HONG KONG, China — A Hong Kong court handed three Tiananmen vigil activists prison sentences of between five and seven years on Friday for national security offenses, drawing international…

blocks.text: HONG KONG, China — A Hong Kong court handed three Tiananmen vigil activists prison sentences of between five and seven years on Friday for national security offenses, drawing international condemnation.
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69; Albert Ho, 74; and Chow Hang-tung, 41, have been behind bars since they were charged in 2021. Their sentences are expected to include the time they have already served.

The United Nations, rights groups and foreign governments have condemned the sentences, issued under a national security law that Beijing imposed on Hong Kong in 2020 following mass pro-democracy protests.
A court ruled in August that the activists had breached the Chinese Constitution by calling for an “end to one-party dictatorship.”
Lee and Chow, who pleaded not guilty, were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months, respectively, AFP journalists in court heard.
Ho, a former lawmaker who pleaded guilty in January, was sentenced to five years and two months.

The verdict held that although the case did not involve violence and the defendants had not put forward a specific timetable to carry out an “end to one-party dictatorship,” their offense was still of “a serious nature.”
Chow, a barrister who represented herself, told a hearing last month that she had “nothing to repent for.”
She raised both arms and waved at supporters as she was escorted out by officers.
Supporters outside court hugged her mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun, who said her daughter had remained in high spirits during the trial.
“She is not a competent barrister. She is simply an outstanding defendant,” her mother said.

Lee crossed himself, smiled and bowed at his wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, and supporters, including the high-profile activist and Cardinal Joseph Zen, who gripped each other’s hands after leaving the courtroom.
“I’m really sad and very angry,” Tang told reporters, saying Lee would “definitely appeal.”
Dozens of police swarmed around the court and set up cordons to hold back crowds.
‘Stern warning’

Hong Kong and Macau were the only places on Chinese soil that permitted public mourning for those killed on June 4, 1989, when Beijing sent troops and tanks to crush protests calling for political reform around the capital’s Tiananmen Square.
But public commemoration has been effectively banned in the cities in recent years.
The trio was among the leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance, the group that organized annual vigils in the city’s Victoria Park.
City leader John Lee said in a statement that “the law will never allow anyone to use the pretext of human rights, democracy and freedom to blatantly harm their own country and compatriots.”
National security police chief Steve Li told reporters the sentences were “a stern warning to those who may be contemplating similar acts.”

Taiwan, which China sees as its own territory, condemned the sentences, while a European Union spokesperson said the ruling “undermines confidence in the rule of law and harms Hong Kong’s reputation.”
UN rights chief Volker Turk “called for these sentences to be quashed,” his office said in a statement.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the “harsh sentences” expose “the cruelty and insecurity of a government afraid of memory and the people.”
Urania Chiu, a legal expert, told AFP that the heavy sentences are “not only [for] overt acts of activism or advocacy, but also acts of remembrance.”
The national security law “is actively shaping what is and is not allowed to remain part of the official history,” she said.
‘Pillar of Shame’
The Hong Kong Alliance group also operated a museum dedicated to the crackdown and held events, including a yearly washing of the “Pillar of Shame” — a statue to mourn victims.
The statue was removed from its longtime plinth at the University of Hong Kong in 2021, and other local universities followed suit with similar objects.
Prosecutors argued that evidence in the case, including the statue and archives from the Hong Kong Alliance’s museum, should be confiscated.
Judge Alex Lee said on Friday the fate of the statue would be decided after a decision was made on its ownership.
The Danish artist behind the “Pillar of Shame,” Jens Galschiot, called the outcome of the trial and the statue’s potential confiscation “outrageous.”
The statue tells the story of Tiananmen, said Galschiot, who has for years sought to reclaim his work.
If destroyed, that would also “destroy the story that everybody should know,” he told AFP. /das

articles.title: Tragic death of woman who testified against father in notorious mafia murder of mother
articles.summary: Denise Cosco testified against the powerful 'Ndrangheta clan and her own father over the murder of her mother in Italy.

blocks.text: A woman who testified against her own father after her mother was murdered in a notorious mafia killing in Italy is believed to have taken her own life.
Denise Cosco was found critically injured on Sunday and died later in hospital in Rome.
Her mother Lea Garofalo, who was killed in 2009, became a powerful symbol of resistance to the mafia after turning witness for the state against the 'Ndrangheta clan in southern Italy.
Those close to Cosco recall her bravery in speaking out at her father's trial, but also her tremendous struggle in the years that followed.
At 35, she died at the same age her mother was when she was murdered.

Enza Rando, a senator and anti-mafia lawyer who represented Cosco at the murder trial, described her death as "a profound wound for the entire country", and proof that the mafia not only kills, but creates "true monsters in the lives and souls" of those who survive.
Francesca Rispoli, co-president of the anti-mafia organisation Libera, said the death highlighted the struggle experienced by many who break with organised crime.

"The mafia, it's not just something physical. You can leave. You can change your name," she told the BBC. "But there is still a tie, a family tie, that stays… deep inside and is impossible to overcome."
Cosco, like her mother, had lived under state protection with a new name and identity for many years.
But Rispoli said she remained extremely vulnerable and had reconnected with her father, Carlo Cosco, in prison in recent years because, despite everything, she had felt a "hole in her life".
Friends say she struggled with mental health problems and addiction.

"Maybe this is a sign that those trying to lead another life need more support. Not just for one year – maybe their whole life," Rispoli argued, as organised crime groups in Italy – especially the 'Ndrangheta - involve close-knit family networks.
In Cosco's case, both her mother's family and her father were tied to the mafia.
She had always refused to believe her father's story that her mother had abandoned her to start a new life in Australia.
In fact, he had tricked Garofalo to a meeting, then had her strangled, her body dismembered then incinerated.
Several years later, a statement by one of the killers finally allowed police to recover some fragments of bone and a necklace, which Cosco identified.
At a public funeral in 2013, she spoke of her mother's courage in "putting herself on the line… for justice for all".
Her father and three accomplices were already serving life in prison.

At the trial, Cosco described herself as a "proud witness for justice" and said she had taken the difficult choice to testify – speaking from behind a screen – because she wanted "inner freedom to start over" with her life.
Prosecutors have now opened an investigation to determine whether there was any incitement to suicide and her phone has been seized for analysis.
Friends and supporters were due to gather in Milan on Friday evening to remember her near the spot where her mother was abducted.
"Denise's entire life revolved between the two extremes of courage and suffering," Luigi Ciotti, president of Libera wrote, calling that a difficult balance.
"Today, something in that fragile equilibrium was broken forever."
If you or someone you know are affected by the issues raised in this story, the BBC Action Line has information on organisations that can offer advice and support.

articles.title: Gaza doc NAZA earns 24.5-minute standing ovation at Venice premiere
articles.summary: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham’s NAZA, a documentary on Israel’s alleged use of AI-assisted military systems to target and kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza, received what's being called the longest…

image.caption: Directors Rachel Szor, left, and Yuval Abraham pose for photographers at the photo call for the film Naza during the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival in Venice on Thursday. (Scott A Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham’s NAZA, a documentary on Israel’s alleged use of AI-assisted military systems to target and kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza, received what's being called the longest standing ovation ever at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.
Documentary has testimony from anonymous Israeli military interviews alleging targeting of civilians in Gaza

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham’s NAZA, a documentary on Israel’s alleged use of AI-assisted military systems to target and kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza, received what's being called a record-breaking 24.5-minute ovation at its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.

Video posted to social media captured the Israeli filmmakers looking solemn — with Abraham appearing to wipe away tears — as the room erupted for the film, which is based on the anonymized testimony of 24 Israeli military insiders.

According to Deadline, it marks the longest-ever standing ovation in Venice, surpassing the near 24-minute rapturous reception for The Voice of Hind Rajab at last year’s festival, and beating the 22-minute ovation for Guillermo del Toro’s dark fantasy piece, Pan’s Labyrinth, when it premiered at Cannes in 2006.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor look drawn and solemn amid strong applause for Golden Lion Contender ‘NAZA’ exposing Israeli targeting of civilians in Gaza #VeniceFilmFestival https://t.co/hqyzoZhwHM—DEADLINE
The Voice of Hind Rajab director Kaouther Ben Hania, who is serving as a juror this year, and its producer Nadim Cheikhrouha were also in attendance for the ovation.
Also in the room were some audience members who unfurled Palestinian and Lebanese flags as the lights came up, according to video posted to social media.

Shot clandestinely under the cover of night from the rooftops in Tel Aviv over a three-year span, NAZA delivers interviews with Israeli military subjects whose identities are obscured. The interviews describe the surveillance systems and AI intelligence the film alleges are being used to identify Hamas targets to bomb their homes, regardless of whether civilian families, including women and children, were inside.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said in a statement that it "categorically rejects" the allegations, and criticized the use of anonymous testimonies which it said "cannot be verified." Regarding the allegations of AI use, it said decisions to strike are made by humans only, and "the IDF strikes military targets and makes unprecedented efforts to minimize harm to civilians."

The film, titled after an acronym the Israeli military used as a shorthand for civilian casualties, is a companion piece to Abraham and Szor’s No Other Land, which won the Academy Award for best documentary in 2025.

Venice Film Festival guests give anti-Israel Gaza film ‘Naza’ longest standing ovation in Venice’s history. The film, which accuses Israel of ‘mass killings of Palestinian civilians,’ received a 24.5 minute long standing ovation from members of the film industry. https://t.co/NMlfFMnFdi—OliLondonTV

NAZA is also executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, who faced intense backlash following his March 2024 Oscar acceptance speech for The Zone of Interest. In the speech, he spoke out against the Israel-Hamas war and stated he and his co-producers stood as men “who refute their Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people.”
When Hamas-led militants attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, some 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 73,422 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in Israel’s ensuing offensive, according to Gaza’s Health ministry. While the ministry does not differentiate between civilians and militants, it says women and children make up half of all casualties.
And civilians are still being killed inside Gaza, Abraham told The Associated Press on Friday.
“What we are showing is something that is very much ongoing,” said Abraham.

“I think our film is showing that this is not some mistake. It’s not an accident. It’s something very, very systemic … and this should have been apparent to everyone, I think, from the start. But we are showing it from the inside, with insider testimony.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.

articles.title: CIA declassifies briefs about al-Qaeda on 9/11 anniversary
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — The CIA released more than 70 presidential intelligence briefs related to al-Qaeda and its leader, Osama bin Laden, on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001,…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — The CIA released more than 70 presidential intelligence briefs related to al-Qaeda and its leader, Osama bin Laden, on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

The release provides “unprecedented transparency into America’s most sensitive intelligence publication from the years before and the day after one of the darkest moments in our history,” the CIA said in a statement.

“The products trace the story of CIA analysts’ evolving understanding of al-Qaeda and efforts to highlight and warn of Osama bin Laden’s attack plotting despite sparse, vague and imperfect information,” it said.
A Sept. 10, 1998, brief — parts of which were redacted — said that al-Qaeda “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a U.S. city.”
Another, dated Dec. 4, 1998, which also contained redactions, said bin Laden “and his allies are preparing for attacks in the U.S., including an aircraft hijacking.”

The briefs cover a period that started during Bill Clinton’s presidency and continued into that of George W. Bush, who was in office when 19 al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four airliners on Sept. 11, 2001.
Two of the jets hit the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers, causing the iconic skyscrapers to collapse.
A third struck the Pentagon, while a fourth — believed to have been headed for Congress or the White House — crashed into a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back.
The United States invaded Afghanistan and later Iraq as part of the so-called “War on Terror” after 9/11 — long-running wars that left tens of thousands of people dead. /das

articles.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
articles.summary: The capture by the rebels of a stretch Yemen's strategic coastline is the group's most impressive military coup for several years.

blocks.text: "Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.
"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."
Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."
"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.
As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.

"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.
"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."

Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".
In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.
Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.
"They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.
But would the US want to get involved anyway?

President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.
According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.

Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".
But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.

Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.

Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".

With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.
For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

articles.title: Stellantis signs MOU with armoured vehicle maker Roshel on potential sale of Brampton, Ont., plant
articles.summary: Automaker Stellantis says it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel on a potential sale of its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.

image.caption: Automaker Stellantis has signed a memorandum of understanding with Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel on a potential sale of the Brampton Assembly Plant. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·Breaking
Automaker Stellantis says it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel on a potential sale of its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.
Move comes as union representing Canadian workers at Stellantis paused contract talks
The move comes as the union representing Canadian workers at Stellantis paused contract talks, citing an impasse over the future of the Brampton plant.

Stellantis spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin says the company considered multiple options for the facility, which has been idled since 2023, and believes Roshel "represents a strong path to restoring sustainable operations."
Unifor is now "actively considering next steps" and says it will provide further details in the days ahead.

items: Stellantis is considering closing and selling Brampton assembly plant, Unifor says

blocks.text: The current collective agreement between the automaker and union is set to expire Sept. 20 at 11:59 p.m.

The talks began Sept. 1 after Unifor ratified new collective agreements with Ford Motor Co. and General Motors in Canada earlier in the summer as part of its pattern bargaining process with each of the Detroit Three.

articles.title: As Poilievre tours U.S., Conservative MP Jamil Jivani bemoans lack of 'alternative to the Liberals'
articles.summary: Conservative MP Jamil Jivani posted a video on social media bemoaning a lack of "an alternative to the Liberals" on Thursday, the same day that his party's leader, Pierre Poilievre, launched a U.S.…

image.caption: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, right, walks with Jamil Jivani, left, in 2024 as the newly-minted MP takes his place in the House of Commons. In a recent video, Jivani said people 'should be offering an alternative to the Liberals, instead going out there to appease people in positions of powe

blocks.text: Politics

Conservative MP Jamil Jivani posted a video on social media bemoaning a lack of "an alternative to the Liberals" on Thursday, the same day that his party's leader, Pierre Poilievre, launched a U.S. tour to argue for tariff-free trade.
Poilievre and Jamil Jivani have disagreed over Canada-U.S. tensions in the past
"You have people who should be offering an alternative to the Liberals, instead going out there to appease people in positions of power," Jivani said in a video posted on X.
The MP went on to say it's his job and the job of the Conservative Party to offer an alternative in Ottawa.

"The reality is there's a great alternative to be putting out there: a vision for Canada where we have a better relationship with the United States, where we avert economic crises, where we build pipelines and infrastructure and we strengthen our economy," he said.

Jivani also argued that the Liberal government is using ongoing tensions with the U.S. to avoid public scrutiny, accused the media of smearing voices critical of Liberal policies as "traitors" and blasted the government for seeking further partnership with China.

We have been here before.

Liberals again want you to believe that to be patriotic is to agree with them and their policies.

They were wrong then.

They are wrong now. pic.twitter.com/Vb28loLSRe—jamiljivani
Jivani didn't mention Poilievre specifically, but the timing of the post prompted former Conservative cabinet minister Jason Kenney to blast the outspoken MP.
In his own post on X, Kenney praised Poilievre for "effectively standing up for Canada and for free trade."

items: As the trade war dominates Canadian politics, Conservatives fight among themselves

blocks.text: He also pointed out that others in the Conservative caucus are amplifying the leader's message and criticized Jivani for not doing the same.

"Instead, he tries to step on Pierre's tour-de-force trip by posting a self-indulgent video casting himself as a martyr, without a kind word to say about his leader's efforts, or a critical word to say about Trump's daily attacks on Canada," Kenney wrote.
Canadians 'confused' by U.S. tactics: Poilievre

Poilievre kicked off his two-day U.S. tour on Thursday, saying in an interview with CNBC that Canadians are "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for the Trump administration.

In a separate interview with BNN Bloomberg on Friday, Poilievre said Canada is standing up for its sovereignty while arguing that building a stronger relationship can buffer both countries against strategic rivals like China.

"By trading more with Canada, we can bring down your cost of living, we can make sure you're supplied for — God forbid — a future conflict, and we can ensure the industrial base of our continent is restored," Poilievre said.

items: 'Unhinged' for Canada to call dispute with U.S. a trade war, says Trump's tariff chief

blocks.text: CBC News has reached out to Poilievre's and Jivani's offices for comment.
Poilievre, who has now made multiple trips south of the border, has refused to criticize Prime Minister Mark Carney in the U.S.
But he has been vocal on the file, calling on the government to recall Parliament, release the details of the rejected trade deal and present a cost-analysis of Canada's counter-tariffs.
The Conservative leader has faced questions about Jivani's comments regarding the U.S. in the past.
Poilievre addresses his MP's comments on Canada having an 'anti-America hissy-fit'
Jivani-Vance friendship
A noted college friend of U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, Jivani has twice travelled to Washington, D.C. to meet with U.S. trade officials.
In an interview with right-wing U.S. media outlet Breitbart News during his first trip in February, Jivani said Canada is "shooting ourselves in the foot if we continue this anti-America hissy-fit."
The comment forced Poilievre to publicly disagree with his MP's characterization of the current tense relationship between the two countries.

"Canadians are legitimately upset by the unjustifiable tariffs and comments that the president has made," Poilievre told reporters at the time, adding that Jivani "speaks for himself [while] I speak for the party."

Days before the latest tariff negotiations fell apart, Vance praised Jivani during a speech at a fundraising event for having "good relationship" with the Trump administration and for being "a pretty effective advocate" for Canada.
In the same speech, Vance called Poilievre a "non-entity" in the trade talks.
When asked about Vance's comments on Jivani, Poilievre said Conservative MPs, and all Canadians, should use the contacts they have to argue for free trade with the U.S.
The day trade talks broke down last month, Jivani accused Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford of putting "their political self-interests ahead of Canadian workers."

The MP later told the National Post that responding to the U.S.'s latest levies on Canadian goods with dollar-for-dollar tariffs would be an "overreaction" — even though dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs were a part of the Conservatives' 2025 platform.
That comment seemed to ruffle at least one other Conservative's feathers. Ontario MP Kyle Seeback reposted the article on X while commenting that Jivani "speaks for no one but himself."
Seeback later deleted the post.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from The Canadian Press
